_provenance.source_pdf: An approach to Jazz Improvisation A method by Peter Bernstein.pdf

usage_notes.narrative: For a minor tonic chord (e.g., Dm as the I chord of a minor-key song), Bernstein prescribes the min6 voicing as the default -- the major 6th replaces the minor 7th -- unless the melody forces a different choice. Chapter 4, p.7.

When the melody explicitly plays the minor 7th of a minor tonic chord, Bernstein prescribes switching from min6 to a min7-type voicing -- specifically using quartal voicings to emphasize both the 7th and the 11th. As he taught: 'the melody plays the minor 7th of the chord, so he suggested playing more of a Dm7-type chord, possibly using quartal voicings to emphasize the 7th and the 11th.' Chapter 4, p.7.

Do not default to min6 when the melody note is the minor 7th of the chord -- the major 6th in a min6 voicing conflicts with the melody's b7. Bernstein's worked example: in a song where 'the melody plays the minor 7th of the chord,' the default Dm6 is overridden and Dm7 (quartal) is prescribed instead. Chapter 4, p.7.

For dom7 (and all chord qualities), Bernstein prescribes beginning with shell voicings -- root, third, and seventh only -- before any extensions or alterations. 'He stopped me and advised me to start with basic chords first--just the root, third, and seventh of each chord ... before making more informed decisions about incorporating chord extensions.' Chapter 5, p.9.

When a melody note risks being doubled by the bass (making it feel weak), Bernstein prescribes voicing the dominant as dom7#11 so the melody note becomes the #11 -- giving it a distinct harmonic 'outfit.' The worked example: 'he prefers to play a B7#11 chord, where the F becomes the #11, allowing the melody note to have a different outfit that enhances its impact and makes it feel good.' Chapter 5, p.9.

On dominant chords that resolve, Bernstein prescribes playing the ii-V a tritone up or down from the original -- 'like playing the related ii chord of the tritone substitution' -- to add harmonic interest during the resolution. Rhythmic placement within the bar is critical: 'playing it in the incorrect position within the bar can create a sense of awkwardness.' Chapter 7, p.13.

Bernstein prescribes a two-phase approach to comping across a tune: start with conservative shell voicings and signature runs only where reliable, then progressively explore extensions and substitutions from the third or fourth chorus onward, after the melody-chord relationships are mapped. 'After playing the third or fourth chorus, he would begin to explore further.' Chapter 4, p.6.

Do not play the root of the I (major tonic) chord. Demonstrated on 'Ornithology': Bernstein showed 'his preference for not playing the roots of the I (one) chords,' choosing instead an I69 derived from the V of that I, which 'adds a unique tension and flavor to the I (one) chord, not resolving the tension fully.' Chapter 6, p.12.

Instead of rooting the I chord, Bernstein prescribes voicing it as an I69 derived from the V chord of that I, deliberately leaving tension partially unresolved. This preserves forward momentum: 'avoiding an excessive emphasis on the I chord is a wonderful way to maintain a sense of forward momentum.' Chapter 6, p.12; Chapter 7, p.13.

Do not overemphasize the I (major tonic) chord. Bernstein teaches: 'when the I chord is overemphasized, it can give the impression that the song is being dragged or held back.' Forward momentum depends on treating the I with restraint -- under-resolve rather than settling. Chapter 7, p.13.

When the I (major tonic) chord is sustained over 2 or 4 measures, Bernstein prescribes actively exploring tension and resolution internally rather than holding a static voicing: 'it becomes essential to explore the play between harmonic tension and resolution within that chord.' Space and rhythm are also key tools within this internal motion. Chapter 6, p.12.

For minor chords as for all chord qualities, Bernstein prescribes starting with root, third, and seventh only before adding extensions. The student is directed to 'focus on listening to the melody and understanding the relationship between the basic chords and the melody before making more informed decisions about incorporating chord extensions.' Chapter 5, p.9.
